findings.note: Product mix and base prices were discoverable quickly from the catalog: plants plus care gear, with clear card prices roughly spanning $12–$52 and out-of-stock status visible.

The footer was where the user first expected shipping, returns, about, privacy, or company trust information, but it only offered a tagline and `hello@fernandfog.example`, which read as placeholder rather than credible contact information.

The product page built some confidence on merchandise details by showing price, stock, difficulty, and care specs, but still omitted shipping cost, returns, guarantee, or policy links near the purchase decision.

Add to cart appeared broken: repeated clicks produced no page change or immediate cart badge update, yet later Cart showed two Golden Pothos, creating silent duplicate additions and undermining confidence in checkout state.
Account felt like a demo form rather than a trust hub: it showed a prefilled demo profile and shipping address, but no order history, policies, shipping rates, or company details.
The user had to enter Checkout to learn full cost; Cart showed only subtotal and Checkout CTA, with no shipping estimate before the payment flow.
Checkout contradicted itself on the money line: it labeled shipping `Free shipping` while charging `$6.00`, with total `$44.00` confirming the charge.
Payment trust was further weakened by `This is a demo shop — no real charge is made.` beside card fields, reinforcing that the shop looked unfinished rather than ready for real card entry.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may make this already-low-trust commerce flow harder to read for some shoppers.

findings.question: What did the user conclude the shop sells, and how quickly was that clear?
findings.answer: It was clear within the first two catalog-scroll steps: Fern & Fog sells houseplants and plant-care gear, including Golden Pothos, Fiddle-Leaf Fig, planters, watering tools, mister, plant food, and shears. Base prices were also visible early, roughly $12–$52, with a starter plant at $19.

findings.question: Which pages or details built trust, and which — if any — eroded it? Quote the specifics.
findings.answer: The catalog and product page built limited trust by making prices, stock, and care details easy to scan. Trust eroded wherever policy or company proof was expected: the footer only said `Questions? hello@fernandfog.example`, Account showed demo data, Cart lacked shipping, and Checkout showed `This is a demo shop — no real charge is made.` plus the contradictory `Free shipping` / `$6.00` line.

findings.question: Did the user hit anything that looked unfinished, inconsistent, or broken while just looking around? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes. Add to cart gave no visible feedback and later produced two cart items; the only email used a `.example` domain; Checkout called shipping `Free shipping` while charging `$6.00`; and the payment form explicitly described the site as a demo shop.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They backtracked from the sparse footer to the header/product flow after failing to find policies, clicked Add to cart twice because nothing changed, detoured into Account looking for trust or policy information, then went through Cart to Checkout because shipping never appeared earlier. The confusion was caused by absent policy links, missing add-to-cart feedback, Cart showing only subtotal, and Checkout’s shipping contradiction.

findings.note: The core catalog was immediately legible: the user understood on the first shop view that Fern & Fog sells houseplants, pots/planters, and care/tools, with category pills where expected.
Product pages built some trust with concrete basics like price, stock, size, care difficulty, drainage/saucer details, and the out-of-stock Fiddle-Leaf note felt honest.
The Price: low to high sort appeared not to reorder the Plants grid; after sorting, the user still saw Monstera, Snake, then Pothos rather than the cheapest item first.

Cart behavior looked broken: add-to-cart did not update the header badge in place, two clicks created quantity 2, quantity was plain text despite copy saying it updates, and Remove did not clear the item.

Shipping and returns were not discoverable where the user expected them: product pages, cart, footer, and Account only exposed a contact email, so the user had to enter Checkout to find shipping at all.
Checkout damaged payment trust by labeling the shipping line “Free shipping” while charging $6.00, producing a $34 total on a $28 subtotal.
Care & Tools lacked potting soil or mix, so the user could not assemble a complete beginner setup from the catalog despite the shop positioning itself as selling plant stuff.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which aligns with the visually soft UI but may make key details like footer/contact, policy gaps, and cart status easier to miss.

findings.question: What did the user conclude the shop sells, and how quickly was that clear?
findings.answer: It was clear immediately from the landing grid and category pills: houseplants, pots/planters, and care/tools. By the end, the user refined that to plants from $19–$52, pots from $14–$32, and care items from $12–$22, with no potting soil/mix.

findings.question: Which pages or details built trust, and which — if any — eroded it? Quote the specifics.
findings.answer: Trust builders were specific product facts: “$19, 15 in stock, 4" nursery pot,” care notes, and the out-of-stock Fiddle-Leaf note. Trust eroders were stronger: footer only showed “hello@fernandfog.example,” cart controls did not work, and Checkout showed “Free shipping” beside “$6.00.”

findings.question: Did the user hit anything that looked unfinished, inconsistent, or broken while just looking around? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes. Sort looked ineffective, the cart badge lagged after add-to-cart, quantity could not be edited despite copy promising it, Remove did not remove the line, and Checkout’s shipping label contradicted the charged amount.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: The main hesitation clustered around cost and trust: the user backtracked from product pages to categories to build a starter basket, then detoured through Cart, Account, and Checkout looking for shipping/returns. Confusion came from static quantity text, no working Remove, no policy links, and the final “Free shipping”/$6 mismatch.

findings.note: Account was the expected and successful entry point: the user immediately chose the top-nav Account link for profile and address updates, and both forms were present there.
Shipping address fields were clear once reached; the note “Checkout starts from this address” made the address-to-checkout relationship explicit before shopping.
Profile save appeared broken: clicking Save profile produced no toast, no field-level status, no signed-in label update, and the email later reverted to riley@example.com after leaving and returning.

Feedback was inconsistent across adjacent account forms: Save address showed a clear “Address saved.” toast and persisted, while Save profile silently did nothing, making the whole account update feel untrustworthy.
The user found no alternate email-change route; Profile Email plus Save profile was the only visible path, so the silent failure blocked the account-update goal entirely.
City and postcode were below the initial fold, but their labels peeked into view and the user correctly inferred scrolling would reveal the rest of Shipping address.
The signed-in email stayed old and was visually easy to miss compared with the editable Email field, so a shopper could falsely believe the profile changed unless they deliberately rechecked it.
Automated accessibility found color-contrast violations, which may further reduce confidence in quiet status text and secondary cues on this otherwise low-contrast page.

findings.question: Did saving the new details visibly succeed, and did the user believe it? What convinced them?
findings.answer: Address saving visibly succeeded and the user believed it because a bottom toast said “Address saved.” and the address fields still held the new values. Profile saving did not visibly succeed: there was no toast or label update, so the user distrusted it and later confirmed it had not persisted.

findings.question: When the user reached checkout, did their updated details carry through, or did they have to re-enter anything?
findings.answer: They never reached checkout. The broken email save stopped the user before shopping or entering payment, so carry-through to checkout was not observed.

findings.question: Could the user confirm the finished order was headed to the new address? How?
findings.answer: No finished order existed. The user could only confirm the account shipping address had saved by seeing the address toast and rechecking the persisted fields after leaving and returning.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Hesitation centered on Profile save: the Save profile button caused no visible change, while the signed-in line still showed the old email. The user backtracked by leaving Shop and returning to Account to test persistence, which exposed the reverted email field.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Save profile was broken or wired to no persistence. The misleading part was that the editable Email field accepted the new address and the button was present, but saving gave no feedback and the account identity stayed old. No alternate email settings or recovery path was visible.

findings.note: Account matched the user’s mental model for both email and shipping: they clicked Account first and immediately found Profile and Shipping address fields where expected.

Shipping address update was discoverable and trustworthy: the street/city/postcode fields were visible in the Shipping address card, Save address was clear, a toast said “Address saved,” and the new address persisted across two leave-and-return checks.

Profile email could not be updated: Save profile produced no visible confirmation and the Email field plus “Signed in as” line reverted to riley@example.com after each reopen, blocking the account-update prerequisite.

Save feedback is inconsistent on the Account page: Save address shows a toast and persists, while Save profile gives no toast, no signed-in-line update, and no error state, making the user distrust the form before discovering the persistence failure.
There was no alternate path for changing email after Profile failed; the sparse header only offered Shop, Cart, and Account, with no settings menu or secondary account-management affordance.

The order portion of the story was never attempted because the user would not proceed while the account email was known to be stale; checkout carry-through and final order confirmation could not be evaluated.
The signed-in line stayed on the old email while the edited Email field temporarily showed the new value, creating a conflicting state that drew attention and prompted re-verification.
Accessibility scan found recurring color-contrast violations, which may further reduce legibility of status, navigation, or form text in this otherwise quiet layout.

findings.question: Did saving the new details visibly succeed, and did the user believe it? What convinced them?
findings.answer: Shipping visibly succeeded: the user saw an “Address saved.” toast and later confirmed 7 Alder Court / Kingsbridge / 6220 persisted. Profile did not visibly succeed: Save profile showed no toast or UI change, and the old signed-in email remained, so the user did not believe it.

findings.question: When the user reached checkout, did their updated details carry through, or did they have to re-enter anything?
findings.answer: They never reached checkout. The blocked profile email update stopped them before ordering, so checkout carry-through was not observed.

findings.question: Could the user confirm the finished order was headed to the new address? How?
findings.answer: No finished order existed. The user could only confirm the saved shipping address on Account after reopening the page; they did not get to an order review or confirmation screen.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Hesitation centered on Profile save. The Email field temporarily showed the new value, but there was no profile toast and the “Signed in as riley@example.com” line stayed old, so the user left and returned twice to verify persistence. The second reversion confirmed the issue rather than resolving confusion.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Save profile appears broken or unwired: it accepts typed input but does not persist it, gives no success or error feedback, and leaves the signed-in identity stale. A real shopper would also notice there is no alternate account/settings route to fix email once that form fails.

findings.note: Catalog narrowing matched the user's mental model: category pills and Price: low to high sort were found in the shop toolbar and supported price-first comparison.
Product-card and detail-page copy gave enough decision support for the final set: Pothos was shelf-friendly and cheap, Terracotta had drainage and saucer, Plant Food was the lowest-cost care item.
Account was expected to provide past orders or plant history, but only profile and shipping appeared; useful account memory existed for checkout prefill, not shopping context.
Product-page Add to cart gave no visible confirmation and the header badge did not update immediately, so normal verification behavior produced duplicate quantities for every selected item.
Cart copy says quantities update when changed, but the Quantity column rendered static plain text with no stepper/input; this blocked correction of the accidental doubles.
Remove was the only cart correction affordance and repeated clicks did not remove the line, leaving the user unable to recover from duplicated items.
Checkout summary showed doubled lines as plain text with no quantity edit or edit-cart link, so the user could only place the wrong $96 order or abandon.
The run recorded 86 color-contrast violation nodes across 8 steps, all from color-contrast; this may compound the already subtle cart/nav feedback issues.

findings.question: Which tools for narrowing and comparing (categories, sorting, search) did the user find, and did each behave as they expected?
findings.answer: They found category pills and sorting where expected in the shop toolbar. Price: low to high behaved as expected and Care & Tools filtering exposed the relevant care items. No search was found or used, but the user did not appear to need it because categories and sorting were sufficient.

findings.question: Did the user compare options before choosing? What information did they lean on, and was any of it missing or unclear?
findings.answer: Yes. They compared plants, pots, and care items mainly on price plus fit-for-purpose copy: shelf-friendly Pothos, drainage/saucer Terracotta, and low-cost Plant Food. The information gap was not product detail; it was order-state clarity after adding items.

findings.question: As the cart grew, did its contents and totals always match what the user had chosen? Note any mismatch.
findings.answer: No. The intended cart was 1x Golden Pothos, 1x Terracotta Pot, and 1x Gentle Plant Food, about $45 before shipping. The cart accumulated 2x of each after silent add actions, reaching subtotal $90 and total $96 at checkout.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Confusion clustered around cart feedback and correction: the product-page badge stayed unchanged after Add, cart quantities appeared as static text despite helper copy promising updates, Remove did nothing, and checkout offered no edit affordance. There was also an early account detour looking for order history that was absent.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Broken: Add to cart did not visibly update the badge, Remove did not remove rows, and no quantity controls existed. Misleading: cart copy promised quantity updates. Missing: checkout lacked an edit-cart or quantity adjustment path, and account lacked expected order history.

findings.note: Golden Pothos Add to cart gave no immediate confirmation and the header stayed at Cart 0 after repeated clicks/Enter, so the user believed the primary commerce action was broken before the cart later showed 3 items.
Cart review said quantities update as you change them, but the user saw only a plain quantity value and Remove, leaving no obvious way to reduce the accidental quantity from 3 to 1.

Unspaced 4242424242424242 was rejected with “Enter the 16-digit number on the card.” even though the field visibly contained 16 digits, making the validation message misleading rather than corrective.
Failed payment submission cleared card number, expiry, and CVC; delivery fields mostly survived, but the prefilled postcode 5041 also failed late with “Enter a 5-digit postcode.”
The spaced card format 4242 4242 4242 4242 with expiry 09/28 and CVC 442 completed the order after postcode was changed to 50410.
Continue shopping from the confirmation screen routed to an empty Checkout page with Cart 0 and a $6 total, not back to the shop catalog.
Payment fields below the fold were discoverable after scrolling, but only Card number was visible initially, so expiry, CVC, and submit were easy to miss on the first checkout viewport.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may make validation and form-state feedback harder to perceive.

findings.question: When the unspaced 16-digit card was submitted, what did the shop say?
findings.answer: It rejected the entry with “Enter the 16-digit number on the card.” A separate late validation error also appeared for the prefilled postcode: “Enter a 5-digit postcode.”

findings.question: Did the unspaced number look like a valid card the user had already typed, or did the message make sense?
findings.answer: It looked like a valid 16-digit number already entered exactly as requested; the message did not explain the real issue, which appeared to be formatting/spaces rather than digit count.

findings.question: Were card / expiry / CVC (and delivery fields) preserved after any rejection?
findings.answer: Card number, expiry, and CVC were cleared after the failed submit. Delivery name, email, street, and city survived; postcode remained present but was rejected until changed from 5041 to 50410.

findings.question: Did the spaced format complete the purchase? Was anything broken or misleading?
findings.answer: Yes, the spaced card completed order FF-1053 after the postcode fix. Broken/misleading items remained: earlier add-to-cart feedback created quantity 3, and Continue shopping after confirmation misrouted to empty checkout showing a $6 total.

findings.note: Opening /checkout directly with Cart 0 worked and landed on the Checkout page, so the route is reachable even when no products have been added.
The user expected checkout access from Cart or top-level navigation, but the header only exposed Shop, Cart 0, and Account; no Checkout control was visible before using the URL.
Empty-cart checkout did not show an empty-state recovery or blocker; it loaded a normal shipping/payment form with an enabled “Place order — $6.00” CTA for zero line items.
The order summary contradicted itself: subtotal was $0.00, the line was labeled “Free shipping,” but it charged $6.00 and made the total $6.00.
Recovery was not obvious on the checkout page: no empty-cart banner, continue-shopping link, or back-to-cart correction path was visible while the form looked like a valid checkout.
Shipping fields were pre-filled despite the empty cart, making the page feel like a real order flow rather than an invalid or recoverable empty-cart state.
No axe-core accessibility violations or console errors were recorded during the run, so the observed problem is product logic and content, not detectable accessibility breakage.

findings.question: With an empty cart, where did opening checkout send the user?
findings.answer: It sent the user directly to http://127.0.0.1:4183/checkout, the normal Checkout page, while the header still indicated Cart 0.

findings.question: What did the page show (message, form, totals)? Was a $6 shipping / pay form offered for no items?
findings.answer: It showed a full checkout form with pre-filled shipping fields, payment inputs, demo no-real-charge copy, subtotal $0.00, shipping shown as $6.00, total $6.00, and an enabled “Place order — $6.00” button. Yes, it offered a $6 shipping-only payment path for no items.

findings.question: Was recovery (back to cart or shop) obvious and correct?
findings.answer: No. The user specifically looked for empty-cart recovery or a blocker, but the visible page presented only the normal checkout flow; no empty-state banner, continue-shopping link, or corrective cart path was apparent.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: checkout is allowed for zero line items, the primary CTA asks for $6.00 anyway, the summary labels that charge “Free shipping,” and the expected empty-cart recovery state is missing. A real shopper would likely notice the inconsistent shipping label and the ability to pay for nothing.

findings.note: Account and Profile were exactly where expected: the header Account link and the Profile card made the email field and Save profile action easy to find.
Invalid email submission produced no visible validation, error banner, field message, button state, request, or DOM change, leaving the user unable to tell whether the save failed or was ignored.

After the invalid save, the form preserved the typed invalid value while the signed-in identity line stayed at the original email, creating a split between editable form state and account identity with no explanation.
Valid email submission was also silent: no success confirmation appeared and the signed-in identity line did not update, so a real shopper could not confirm receipts would go to the new address.
No accessibility violations or console errors were recorded, so the observed failure is primarily product feedback/state communication rather than technical page breakage.

findings.question: After saving the invalid email, what exactly appeared on screen (error, success, nothing)?
findings.answer: Nothing appeared: no error, success message, toast, field-level validation, or button feedback was visible.

findings.question: Did the form keep the invalid email the user typed, reset to the old value, or clear fields?
findings.answer: The Email field kept `not-an-email`; it did not reset or clear. The separate signed-in line still showed `riley@example.com`.

findings.question: After the valid email save, was success visible, and did the field show the new address?
findings.answer: Success was not visible. The Email field showed `riley.fixed@example.com`, but the signed-in line still showed the old address.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes. The same silent behavior occurred for both invalid and valid saves, so shoppers would not know whether an email was rejected, saved, or only edited locally. The unchanged signed-in email makes the valid save especially ambiguous.

findings.note: Product discovery and the primary purchase controls were where expected: the Calathea card was visible in the shop grid, and stock, quantity, and Add to cart were prominent on the product page.

Full-stock add was refused even though requested quantity equaled the stock line; the message said "Only 5 in stock — you can add 5 more" while leaving Cart at 0, which reads as internally contradictory.
Stock-minus-one add succeeded silently: qty 4 later appeared in the cart, but the product page gave no confirmation and initially left the user believing Cart was still 0.
After 4 units were in cart, adding 1 more showed "Only 5 in stock — you can add 1 more" but did not add the fifth unit, so the refusal message claimed availability while blocking the action.
The product stock line stayed "In stock — 5 available" after 4 units were in the cart, contradicting the remaining purchasable quantity and making the "you can add N more" text harder to trust.

Feedback under the Add to cart button was visually small and soft pink on a calm product page; it existed, but the user repeatedly relied on the cart badge/cart page to determine whether the action worked.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which aligns with the visually low-emphasis error/refusal feedback observed during the run.

findings.question: Could the user add exactly the full remaining stock in one add? What did the shop say?
findings.answer: No. Qty 5 was refused with: "Only 5 in stock — you can add 5 more." Cart stayed at 0 after that attempt.

findings.question: Did any error message's "you can add N more" arithmetic match the stock line and cart?
findings.answer: No. The message echoed the requested quantity rather than the true remaining capacity: it said 5 more when cart was 0 and stock was 5, then later said 1 more when cart already held 4 but did not allow that one to land.

findings.question: After maxing the cart, what happened when they tried one more unit?
findings.answer: The cart never actually reached 5. After 4 units were in cart, adding 1 more showed "Only 5 in stock — you can add 1 more" and Cart stayed at 4.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: full-stock add was blocked with contradictory copy; qty 4 succeeded without product-page confirmation; stock stayed at 5 available after cart held 4; the final available unit could not be added; and the only feedback was a low-emphasis inline message rather than a clear success/refusal state.

findings.note: The catalog presents a role=search region and a Search button, but no visible query text field; the user expected a field next to Sort/Search and could only create the nonce search by manually navigating to `?q=zxqq9-no-such-plant-ever`.

Clicking the visible Search button did not open a search field or search UI; it only changed the URL to `?sort=`, leaving the full catalog unchanged and deepening the mismatch between label and behavior.
The empty-results state itself was easy to recognize once reached: the no-match headline, empty panel, and underlined `Clear the search` link visually dominated the page.
The `Clear the search` recovery link is broken: after two clicks, the URL still included `?q=zxqq9-no-such-plant-ever`, the no-results copy remained, and no products reappeared.

The empty-results copy mixes shopper-facing language with implementation jargon: `No matches for...` and `Clear the search to browse everything` are clear, but `Query returned no product rows for the given term` exposes database phrasing.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may further reduce discoverability of subtle toolbar and link affordances.

findings.question: What exact empty-results message did the user see for the nonce search?
findings.answer: They saw: `No matches for “zxqq9-no-such-plant-ever”.`, `Query returned no product rows for the given term.`, and `Clear the search to browse everything.` with a `Clear the search` link.

findings.question: Was the message plain-language help or jargon a shopper would not understand?
findings.answer: Mixed. The no-match headline and clear instruction are plain language, but `Query returned no product rows for the given term` is database-style jargon rather than shopper-facing help.

findings.question: After clicking clear/recovery, did products reappear, or did the empty state persist?
findings.answer: The empty state persisted after both clicks; the URL stayed on `?q=zxqq9-no-such-plant-ever` and no product grid returned.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: the catalog had a Search button but no visible text input for entering a query, the Search button did not reveal one, and the `Clear the search` link did not clear the failed search. A shopper would also notice the internal-sounding `product rows` copy.

findings.note: Product detail had the expected quantity field and prominent Add to cart CTA, so the initial add path was easy to find.

Add-to-cart feedback was unreliable: repeated clicks left the header badge at 0 with no toast or inline confirmation, then the cart later showed 4 items, making the user think the control had failed before discovering it had over-added.
Cart copy promised “Quantities update as you change them,” but the quantity column was static text, leaving no visible way to reduce 4× Monstera to a budget-fitting count.
The only cart-row edit control, Remove, did nothing across repeated attempts, blocking the user from clearing the over-budget line item.
Cart showed subtotal but not shipping, so the user had to enter checkout to verify the all-in budget math.
Checkout order summary was read-only and lacked an edit-cart affordance, so the user could see the over-budget total but not fix it before payment.
Checkout labeled shipping “Free shipping” while charging $6.00, creating a direct trust break in the final total.
Fallback surfaces did not rescue the workflow: product detail only allowed adding more, Account only had profile/address forms, and Shop had no clear-cart or mini-cart control.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may worsen discoverability of quiet nav and secondary controls in this already fragile cart workflow.

findings.question: Could the user change quantities and remove items where they expected to? Describe any edit that fought back.
findings.answer: No. The user expected quantity editing and Remove on the cart; quantity was static text despite help copy, and Remove did not change the row. Product and checkout offered no alternate reduce/remove path.

findings.question: After each cart change, did every number on screen (line totals, subtotal, cart badge, checkout total) stay consistent? Note any lag or mismatch.
findings.answer: No. The badge appeared stuck at 0 after Add-to-cart attempts, then later showed 4, revealing a feedback lag or mismatch. Once stuck, line total/subtotal/checkout total consistently reflected 4× Monstera, but they could not be changed.

findings.question: Did the user trust the final total matched their budget arithmetic? Why or why not?
findings.answer: They trusted it was over budget, but not the store’s pricing integrity: $152 subtotal plus a $6 line produced $158, while the shipping label said “Free shipping.” That contradiction made the final total feel misleading.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They hesitated after Add-to-cart showed no visible result, backtracked from checkout to cart because the summary was read-only, retried Remove after returning to cart, then searched Account and Shop for rescue controls. The causes were absent quantity inputs, dead Remove, no checkout edit link, and misleading shipping copy.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Broken: Remove did nothing and Add-to-cart feedback/badge behavior was misleading. Missing: editable quantity controls, checkout edit-cart link, clear-cart path, and cart-level shipping/all-in total. Misleading: “Quantities update as you change them” and “Free shipping” with a $6 charge.

findings.note: The product page matched the first add-to-cart expectation: quantity and the green Add to cart CTA were prominent and easy to find.
Add to cart appeared to do nothing on the product page: repeated clicks and a quantity change left the header at Cart0 with no toast or inline confirmation, even though the cart later showed 4 items.
The header Cart badge eventually became the strongest bag affordance once it changed to Cart4, pulling the user naturally into the cart to inspect totals.
The cart was the expected place to trim, but the quantity column showed static text despite copy saying “Quantities update as you change them,” and Remove was the only visible edit action.
Remove fought the user: two clicks produced no visible change to item count, line total, subtotal, or cart badge, leaving 4x Stoneware Planter at $128.
Checkout did not provide a fallback edit path; the order summary exposed the over-budget total but offered only static line items and totals.
Checkout undermined budget trust by labeling shipping “Free shipping” while adding $6.00, taking the total from $128 to $134.
After checking cart, checkout, the product page, header navigation, and account, the user found no working way to drop items or reduce quantity, so the budgeted order could not be placed.
Accessibility scan found color-contrast violations across two captured steps, which may make already-muted prices, links, or secondary controls harder to notice.

findings.question: Could the user change quantities and remove items where they expected to? Describe any edit that fought back.
findings.answer: No. The user expected quantity controls in the cart, then checkout, then the product page. The cart showed only static quantity text, and Remove was clicked twice with no effect.

findings.question: After each cart change, did every number on screen (line totals, subtotal, cart badge, checkout total) stay consistent? Note any lag or mismatch.
findings.answer: Numbers did not behave consistently. Add to cart left the badge at Cart0 on the product page, but later the header/cart showed Cart4. Remove did not update any visible number. Checkout subtotal matched the stuck cart, but shipping labeling contradicted the charge.

findings.question: Did the user trust the final total matched their budget arithmetic? Why or why not?
findings.answer: No. The user could see the order was over budget ($128 subtotal, $134 total), but could not trust or act on the arithmetic because cart edits failed and “Free shipping” still added $6.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Confusion clustered around controls that looked actionable but did not change state: Add to cart with no badge/confirmation, cart copy promising quantity updates beside static text, Remove with no effect, and checkout summary without edit controls.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Broken: Remove did nothing and Add to cart feedback lagged or failed. Misleading: cart copy promised quantity editing, and checkout said “Free shipping” while charging $6. Missing: quantity controls or any clear-cart/edit path in cart or checkout.

findings.note: The apparent search area matched the user's first expectation, but it was not typeable; the user abandoned search only because the desired Snake Plant card was already visible in the grid.
Product discovery itself worked once browsing: Snake Plant was visually prominent in the top row, and the product page's green Add to cart CTA was exactly where the user expected it.
Add to cart gave no visible success state and the header badge still appeared to show 0, so the user repeated the action and accidentally put two plants in the cart.
Cart recovery failed: the page promised quantity updates but showed static quantity text, and repeated Remove clicks had no effect, leaving the user forced to checkout with two plants instead of one.
Checkout layout was understandable but payment fields began below the fold; the user had to scroll after entering card number to find expiry, CVC, and Place order.
A delivery validation failure wiped all payment fields, making the user re-enter card number, expiry, and security code before retrying.
Postcode validation messaging was confusing: the page still showed “Enter a 5-digit postcode” after a five-digit value was entered, then cleared later without an explicit explanation.
The usual-card failure provided no visible decline, error banner, or charge-status message; the user inferred failure only because they remained on checkout with no confirmation.
The final confirmation page was unambiguous: order number, confirmed status, delivery address, receipt note, total, and cart reset were all visible.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may make already-subtle validation and form-state cues harder to perceive.

findings.question: When the payment failed, what exactly did the shop tell the user, and did they understand what had happened and whether they'd been charged?
findings.answer: It told them nothing visible about the card failure. The user stayed on checkout with no confirmation, no decline message, and no charge-status reassurance, so they inferred failure from lack of progress and switched to the backup card without certainty about whether the first attempt charged.

findings.question: How much did the user have to re-enter to try again? Name anything the form forgot.
findings.answer: After the postcode validation failure, the form forgot the full payment section: card number, expiry, and security code. The user also replaced the postcode before re-entering payment details.

findings.question: Did the user finish the purchase, and how sure were they that it succeeded exactly once?
findings.answer: They finished checkout with the backup card and reached a clear confirmation for order FF-1053. They could be sure one order was confirmed, but not that the purchase matched intent, because the order was Snake Plant ×2 and the first failed card attempt gave no explicit not-charged message.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They hesitated at search because the expected search input was not typeable; on product/cart because cart count and feedback did not match Add to cart; in cart because quantity looked static and Remove did nothing; at checkout because postcode validation persisted after valid-looking input and payment failure had no message.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: the search affordance lacked a usable input, Add to cart lacked confirmation, cart quantity controls were missing despite helper text, Remove did not work, delivery validation wiped payment fields, postcode error copy was misleading, and failed payment lacked decline/not-charged feedback.

findings.note: Care items were discoverable once the user moved from Account to Shop: the Care & Tools pill was visually obvious, and the product detail page clearly exposed stock, quantity, and Add to cart for Gentle Plant Food.
Account was the user's first expected home base for reordering, but it only contained Profile and Shipping; absence of order history caused an initial detour before shopping.
Add to cart gave no visible confirmation and the header badge still appeared as 0, so the user clicked twice and accidentally created a 16-item cart instead of the intended 8.

Cart correction was effectively blocked: the page said quantities update as changed, but quantity displayed as non-editable plain text, and Remove did nothing across clicks, leaving the user stuck with 16 items.

Checkout payment validation was misleading: a continuous 16-digit card stayed red with “Enter the 16-digit number on the card,” only succeeding after the user inferred the placeholder-required spaced format.
Failed Place order attempts wiped payment fields, forcing the user to re-enter card, expiry, and CVV multiple times while trying to recover from validation errors.
Saved Account data contained postcode 5041, but checkout required a 5-digit postcode; the user discovered this only on submit and had to alter saved shipping data to continue.
The confirmation page's “View your orders” link sent the user to /account#orders, but Account still showed only Profile and Shipping with no order history or FF-1053 receipt.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may worsen visibility of subtle affordances like cart badges, helper text, and low-emphasis links.

findings.question: How did the user discover how many of an item they could actually buy, and was the shop upfront about it or did they find out the hard way?
findings.answer: They discovered stock on the product detail page: Gentle Plant Food showed 18 available before adding to cart, so availability for 8 was upfront. The hard-way discovery was not stock capacity but cart state: no add confirmation made them believe 8 had not been added, producing an accidental 16.

findings.question: When the shop couldn't meet the request, what did it offer the user to work with, and how did they adapt?
findings.answer: The shop actually could meet the 8-item request based on stock. It offered no meaningful adaptation path when the cart became wrong: no editable quantity, no working Remove, and no suggested alternatives. The user adapted by checking out with 16 of the same item because that was the only placeable cart state.

findings.question: Did the user lose any work (cart contents, typed input) at any point while adapting? Describe it.
findings.answer: Yes. Payment input was repeatedly wiped after failed Place order attempts, forcing re-entry of card number, expiry, and CVV. The cart contents were not lost; instead they were stuck at the wrong quantity.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They backtracked from Account after finding no order history, hesitated after Add to cart because the badge stayed 0 with no toast, got stuck in Cart because quantity looked like static text and Remove had no effect, and later looped in Checkout because the card field showed an error despite 16 digits. After ordering, they also re-scrolled Account because #orders implied an order list that was not present.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Broken: Remove did not remove, quantity could not be edited, payment fields wiped after failed submit, and View your orders landed on a missing order-history section. Misleading: cart copy promised quantity updates, card helper asked for a 16-digit number while rejecting continuous 16 digits, and saved postcode passed Account but failed Checkout. Missing: add-to-cart confirmation and Account order history.

findings.note: The user’s first expectation was correct: Care & Tools was the natural home for a small plant-care gift item, and Gentle Plant Food was quickly identified as the cheapest suitable option.
Listing cards did not show stock or maximum purchasable quantity, so the user had to open product detail to learn whether eight units were possible.

After selecting “Price: low to high,” the visual order still appeared to start with the watering can, making the sort feel unreliable even though the user could still find the cheapest item by reading prices.
The product page did provide the key stock answer clearly: “In stock — 18 available,” so the user learned eight Gentle Plant Food units should be allowed before adding to cart.
Add to cart gave no confirmation and the header badge stayed at Cart0 after a successful add, causing the user to click again and accidentally create a quantity of 16.
Cart recovery was blocked: the cart promised “Quantities update as you change them,” but quantity was static text, and repeated Remove clicks did not change the row, subtotal, or badge.

Neither the product page nor checkout offered a way to edit, replace, or clear the stuck cart line; checkout only presented locked ×16 totals and payment fields, so the user reasonably refused to place the order.
Account was a plausible but dead-end recovery path for a shopper looking for saved-cart or session controls; it only exposed profile and shipping forms.
Accessibility scan found color-contrast violations on two steps, which may worsen scannability of secondary controls such as category pills, header badge, or cart actions.

findings.question: How did the user discover how many of an item they could actually buy, and was the shop upfront about it or did they find out the hard way?
findings.answer: They discovered the limit on the product detail page, where Gentle Plant Food showed “In stock — 18 available.” That was upfront once they opened the item, but not upfront on the listing cards, where they expected stock or max quantity before drilling in.

findings.question: When the shop couldn't meet the request, what did it offer the user to work with, and how did they adapt?
findings.answer: The shop did not fail the stock request: it could sell eight because 18 were available. The failure was cart control after a duplicate add; the shop offered no usable adaptation path beyond Remove, Account, and checkout, none of which let the user return to eight.

findings.question: Did the user lose any work (cart contents, typed input) at any point while adapting? Describe it.
findings.answer: They did not lose typed checkout/profile input; the final checkout still showed saved customer details. They effectively lost the intended cart state: eight units became sixteen after a second add caused by stale feedback, and the user could not restore the intended quantity.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Confusion centered on the mismatch between screen copy and controls: Cart0 after adding, cart text claiming quantities update while showing plain-text “16,” Remove not changing anything, and checkout showing a locked ×16 summary. The user backtracked through product, cart, Account, and checkout looking for an edit or clear-cart path.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: stale cart badge, no add confirmation, non-editable cart quantity despite copy saying quantities update, Remove apparently nonfunctional, no clear-cart/edit path on product or checkout, and stock absent from listing cards. The “Free shipping $6.00” line on checkout also reads internally inconsistent.

findings.note: The cart body has no page-local continue-shopping equivalent; a shopper scanning below line items and near subtotal/Checkout finds no recovery path back to catalog except leaving the cart content for global navigation.

Add to cart gave misleading feedback: repeated clicks on an in-stock Snake Plant left the visible header badge at 0 with no toast or success state, but later the cart contained quantity 2, meaning the action succeeded invisibly and duplicated the item.
Product cards on the catalog behaved as full-card links rather than offering grid-level add-to-cart, so the user had to open a detail page before adding an in-stock plant.
Once on /cart, cart state was internally consistent: header showed Cart2, the line item was Snake Plant, quantity/total implied two units, and subtotal matched $52.00.
The final accessibility capture reported color-contrast violations, which may further weaken secondary navigation and status readability around this sparse cart view.

findings.question: Was there a continue-shopping (or equivalent) control in the cart page body?
findings.answer: No. The cart body showed the heading, helper text, line item table, subtotal, Checkout, and footer, but no `Continue shopping`, `Keep shopping`, `Back to shop`, or similar body control.

findings.question: If yes, where did it go? If no, what options remained to keep shopping?
findings.answer: Only global navigation remained: the header `Shop` link and the Fern & Fog brand link. The user correctly did not click or invent a local cart-body path.

findings.question: Did the cart contents and badge stay consistent while checking?
findings.answer: On the cart page, yes: the badge read Cart2 and the cart showed Snake Plant at quantity 2 with a $52.00 subtotal. The inconsistency was earlier, when the badge appeared stuck at 0 after add clicks that later had taken effect.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Missing: the cart-body continue-shopping path. Misleading: add-to-cart appeared not to work because the badge and page did not visibly update, yet the cart later contained two units. Also, catalog cards lacked direct add buttons, adding an extra product-detail step.

findings.note: The Account entry point itself was discoverable: the user found and clicked the header Account link immediately from the shop homepage.

The expected destination, Account, appeared to be profile settings only: Profile and Shipping Address dominated, with no Order history, Past orders, order numbers, status badges, or receipt links after full-page scrolling.
Global navigation did not offer a recovery path for orders: the header exposed only Shop, Cart, and Account, so the user had no visible Orders/History affordance once Account lacked the section.
Common order-history routes and nested account-history routes all dead-ended in 404s, so URL guessing did not reveal a hidden but reachable order history.
The direct seeded-order receipt attempts failed, including `/order/FF-1041`; the user could not open FF-1041 or FF-1052 to inspect status or ETA.
The `/order/FF-1041` error copy said “Your order history lives in your account,” contradicting the Account page that contained no order-history UI.
404 recovery was weak for this task: the failure state offered only “Back to the shop,” not a link to Account or orders despite mentioning account-hosted history.
The shop catalog and footer were product-only; the final scan found product cards plus brand/email text, with no orders or receipt affordance.
Accessibility scan found recurring color-contrast violations, which may further reduce discoverability for low-vision shoppers even though the primary blocker was missing order history.

findings.question: Which past order did the user open, and what status did the shop show?
findings.answer: No past order was opened. Attempts to reach FF-1041 directly failed, and no UI exposed FF-1041 or FF-1052, so no status was shown.

findings.question: What exact delivery estimate / ETA text appeared on the receipt?
findings.answer: No receipt was reached, so no delivery estimate or ETA text appeared.

findings.question: Did status and ETA agree for a shipped or delivered order?
findings.answer: This could not be assessed because the user never reached a shipped or delivered receipt. The study only establishes that the receipt path was undiscoverable/unreachable.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: Account lacked any order-history section despite being the expected path; header/footer had no Orders or History link; common history URLs and direct receipt URLs 404ed; and `/order/FF-1041` misleadingly claimed order history lives in Account while Account showed only Profile and Shipping.

findings.note: Account was the expected location for order history, but it exposed only Profile and Shipping address; no Orders, Order history, Past orders, receipt list, or secondary account navigation appeared after full-page inspection.
The missing Account affordance forced URL guessing: /account/orders, /orders, /orders/FF-1041, and /account/orders/FF-1041 all failed, so the seeded shipped/delivered receipts were not discoverable.
404 recovery was empty for this task: each failed order path showed only a generic not-found message and “Back to the shop,” with no link to Account, Orders, tracking, support, or receipt lookup.

Because no past-order receipt could be opened, the user could not quote status or ETA copy, and the team cannot validate whether old orders show stale “confirmed · arrives in 3–5 days” messaging from this path.
The Account page’s visual hierarchy reinforced the wrong model: profile and shipping forms plus green Save buttons dominated, making Account feel like settings rather than a customer purchase hub.
The global Account link was where the user expected and was used immediately from the homepage, so top-level Account discoverability itself was not the blocker.
No axe-core accessibility violations were reported across the run, so the failure appears to be information architecture/routing rather than basic accessibility compliance.

findings.question: Which past order did the user open, and what status did the shop show?
findings.answer: No past order was opened. The user attempted FF-1041 through /orders/FF-1041 and /account/orders/FF-1041, but both paths 404ed, so no shop status was shown.

findings.question: What exact delivery estimate / ETA text appeared on the receipt?
findings.answer: No ETA text appeared because no receipt page was reachable.

findings.question: Did status and ETA agree for a shipped or delivered order?
findings.answer: This could not be evaluated: neither status nor ETA was displayed for a shipped or delivered order.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes. Account lacked any order-history entry point; common order list and receipt URLs returned generic 404s; and the 404 page offered only “Back to the shop,” not a path to orders, tracking, or support.

findings.note: The Sort control was discoverable in the expected toolbar location above the category pills, next to Search; the user found and changed it immediately from the catalog page.

Selecting "Price: low to high" updated the combobox and URL to `?sort=price-asc`, but the grid stayed in Featured order: Monstera $38, Snake Plant $26, Golden Pothos $19, with cheaper Terracotta Pot $14 still mid-grid.
Selecting "Price: high to low" also updated state without reordering the grid; Fiddle-Leaf Fig $52 should have led but remained fifth, confirming the product list ignores price sort entirely.
The page gives no visible confirmation that the grid changed after sorting beyond the combobox value, making the broken sort look like a valid applied state until the shopper manually checks prices.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations across the run; muted price text may be harder to read for some shoppers even though this user could extract the prices.

findings.question: What were the first three products/prices before sorting?
findings.answer: Monstera Deliciosa — $38.00; Snake Plant — $26.00; Golden Pothos — $19.00.

findings.question: What were the first three after sorting Price low to high?
findings.answer: They were unchanged: Monstera Deliciosa — $38.00; Snake Plant — $26.00; Golden Pothos — $19.00.

findings.question: Did the grid order actually change to match the selected sort?
findings.answer: No. Low-to-high did not put the cheapest item first, and high-to-low did not put the most expensive item first; the same first three remained in place.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: The Sort control and URL reflected the chosen price sort, but the product grid ignored it. A shopper comparing prices would see Terracotta Pot $14 below higher-priced items in low-to-high and Fiddle-Leaf Fig $52 below cheaper items in high-to-low.

findings.note: Product discovery worked well: the Monstera was the first card in the shop grid under “Everything,” matching where the user expected to find it.
The product page put the expected controls in the right place: quantity defaulted to 1, stock was visible, and the green “Add to cart” button was the obvious primary action.

The primary purchase action appeared to be a silent no-op: after clicking “Add to cart,” the user remained on the product page, the cart badge stayed at 0, and no toast, inline confirmation, or redirect appeared.
Because the item never entered the cart, checkout and order confirmation were unreachable; the user could not prove the birthday gift was purchased before closing the tab.
No axe-core accessibility violations were recorded across the run, so the observed failure was functional/trust-related rather than an accessibility blocker.

findings.question: How did the user try to find the monstera, and how directly did the shop take them to it?
findings.answer: They scanned the shop grid and found “Monstera Deliciosa” immediately as the first product card under “Everything,” then opened its product page directly. Discovery was fast and aligned with expectation.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Confusion began only after the first add-to-cart click: the user expected a cart count change, confirmation, or redirect, but the page stayed unchanged and the header still showed Cart0.

findings.question: Did every action produce a visible confirmation it had worked? Name any that did not.
findings.answer: No. Opening the product page worked visibly, but clicking “Add to cart” did not produce any visible confirmation; the cart badge remained 0 and no success message appeared.

findings.question: Could the user prove to themselves the order was placed? How?
findings.answer: No. They never got an item into the cart, reached checkout, or saw an order confirmation, so there was no proof of purchase.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: The “Add to cart” button on an in-stock Monstera with quantity 1 appeared broken or disconnected. A real shopper would notice the unchanged Cart0 badge and missing confirmation immediately, especially before entering payment details.

findings.note: The search area looked like the fastest path, but the apparent search control was not a text field; the user expected to type near Sort/Search and had to abandon search for browsing.
The product grid rescued discovery: Monstera Deliciosa was visually prominent as the first card, so the user could still reach the product page directly after search failed.
Add to cart lacked immediate visible confirmation: the header badge stayed at 0 and there was no toast or button state, so the user clicked again and unknowingly added two plants.
The cart showed Monstera ×2 with no obvious quantity controls, leaving the user to proceed with the wrong quantity under time pressure.
Checkout layout was mostly predictable, but the pay action and remaining payment fields were below the fold after card entry, adding a scroll before the user could complete payment.
Postcode validation was misleading: five-digit values such as 50412 and 12345 still showed “Enter a 5-digit postcode,” so the message did not explain the actual requirement or state.
Payment validation blocked completion: a 16-digit card number repeatedly showed “Enter the 16-digit number on the card,” Place order never left checkout, and no confirmation page appeared.
After failed submits, payment fields appeared filled visually but the captured form values were empty, creating a state mismatch that made recovery confusing and unreliable.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which matters here because key validation feedback relies on red/pink error styling.

findings.question: How did the user try to find the monstera, and how directly did the shop take them to it?
findings.answer: They first tried free-text search near the Sort/Search row, but that control was not fillable. Discovery still became direct because the Monstera card was already first in the grid and easy to click.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: Confusion clustered around controls that looked actionable but gave bad feedback: non-fillable search, add-to-cart with no badge/toast change, cart quantity shown as plain text, postcode errors that persisted on five digits, and card errors that persisted on a 16-digit value.

findings.question: Did every action produce a visible confirmation it had worked? Name any that did not.
findings.answer: No. Add to cart did not visibly confirm until the user opened cart, causing a double-add. Place order also never confirmed success; it kept the user on checkout with validation errors and emptied/desynced payment state.

findings.question: Could the user prove to themselves the order was placed? How?
findings.answer: No. They never reached a confirmation page, receipt, order number, or changed checkout state. The final page remained checkout with empty payment values and a card validation error.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: misleading search UI, silent add-to-cart feedback, missing cart quantity controls, duplicate quantity caused by retrying, misleading postcode validation, broken card validation, payment field value desync after submit, and contrast issues around visual feedback.

findings.note: Product discovery worked well: the user found an in-stock Snake Plant from the homepage grid and the product page matched their expectations for price, stock, quantity, and Add to cart placement.
Add to cart gave no immediate feedback on the product page: the header stayed at Cart 0 after clicks, causing the user to click again and accidentally add two plants.
The cart trapped the user at quantity 2: the page promised “Quantities update as you change them,” but quantity appeared as non-editable plain text with no stepper or input.
The cart’s only visible recovery action, Remove, did not clear the item when attempted, leaving qty 2 / $52 and blocking correction of the accidental double-add.
Checkout exposed a static order summary with Snake Plant ×2 but no edit or remove affordance, so it confirmed the problem without offering recovery before payment.
Checkout summary labeled shipping as “Free shipping” while showing a $6.00 charge, a credibility issue the user noticed while already doubting the cart.
Account was a plausible but unsuccessful fallback: after scrolling, it only contained profile and shipping address fields, with no cart management or order controls.
The payment-failure recovery story was never reached because cart correction failed first; the user abandoned rather than risk paying for two plants.

findings.question: When the payment failed, what exactly did the shop tell the user, and did they understand what had happened and whether they'd been charged?
findings.answer: Payment was never attempted, so no failure message, charge status, or user understanding of a declined card was observed. The cart issue blocked the study before the temperamental card path.

findings.question: How much did the user have to re-enter to try again? Name anything the form forgot.
findings.answer: Not observed. The user never submitted payment or retried with the backup card; no evidence about retained or forgotten checkout fields was produced.

findings.question: Did the user finish the purchase, and how sure were they that it succeeded exactly once?
findings.answer: No. They gave up explicitly because the cart was stuck at two Snake Plants and they were unwilling to risk a duplicate purchase; certainty of exactly-once success was therefore zero.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They backtracked from cart to checkout, cart, product, cart, and account because the cart showed qty 2 as plain text, Remove did not work, checkout was static, and the product page only offered another Add action that would increase the quantity.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: Add to cart feedback/badge lag was misleading, cart quantity editing was missing despite copy promising it, Remove appeared broken, checkout lacked item edit/remove controls, and “Free shipping” showed a $6.00 charge.

findings.note: Product summary contains a high-prominence contradiction: the availability line says "In stock — more arriving daily" immediately above a disabled purchase button labeled "Out of stock."

Secondary availability and description copy align with the disabled button, saying the next batch is on the way / check back soon, which makes the green "In stock" line look like stale or incorrectly mapped inventory text.
The expected path worked: the user found the required product via the Fiddle-Leaf Fig card in the shop grid and did not need search, URL entry, or another product detour.
The disabled button behavior was technically consistent with its state: the click attempt was refused because the control was disabled.
No axe-core accessibility violations were reported across the run.

findings.question: What did the stock / availability line say, quoted?
findings.answer: The main stock line said "In stock — more arriving daily." The page also said "The next batch is on its way from the greenhouse — check back soon."

findings.question: What did the purchase button say, and was it enabled or disabled?
findings.answer: The main purchase button said "Out of stock" and was disabled.

findings.question: Did label and control state agree, or contradict each other?
findings.answer: The button label and disabled state agreed with each other, but contradicted the main "In stock" availability line.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes. A shopper would see an in-stock claim directly above a disabled out-of-stock buy button, while other copy says to check back soon. The misleading part is the primary stock line, not the button behavior.

findings.note: The product card/listing path matched expectation: the user saw Fiddle-Leaf Fig in the shop grid and opened the requested detail page without trying other products.

The product page presents conflicting purchase signals: availability says "In stock — more arriving daily" while the primary CTA is disabled and labeled "Out of stock"; supporting copy also says the item is sold out/check back soon.
The disabled CTA correctly blocked the attempted purchase click, but the blocked state exposed the contradiction rather than resolving it because the nearby stock line still claimed availability.

findings.question: What did the stock / availability line say, quoted?
findings.answer: It said: "In stock — more arriving daily". Nearby copy also said the next batch was on its way and to check back soon.

findings.question: What did the purchase button say, and was it enabled or disabled?
findings.answer: The main purchase button said "Out of stock" and was disabled.

findings.question: Did label and control state agree, or contradict each other?
findings.answer: The button label and disabled state agreed with each other, but they contradicted the stock line claiming "In stock — more arriving daily".

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: availability messaging was misleading. The page simultaneously claimed in-stock availability, told the shopper to check back because the next batch was coming, and disabled purchase as out of stock; the attempted click was blocked as expected for a disabled control.

findings.note: The product catalog supported the initial item choice well: Gentle Plant Food was visible as a cheap in-stock option and matched the story example.
Product-page Add to cart appeared to do nothing: repeated clicks left the user on the same page with Cart 0 and no toast, while the cart later revealed all clicks had actually added items.
Cart quantity was not editable despite copy saying quantities update as changed; the row showed a static quantity of 3 with only Remove available.
Remove did not work after two clicks, so the user could not correct the unintended quantity and had to proceed with 3 units instead of one.
Checkout was prefilled with postcode 5041 but validation required 5 digits, blocking order placement and forcing the user to invent a corrected postcode.
Failed checkout validation cleared the card number, expiry, and CVC, adding re-entry friction after an unrelated delivery-field error.
Order summary repeatedly labeled shipping as "Free shipping" while charging $6.00, including after cart-empty return where subtotal was $0.00 and total was $6.00.
The confirmation page made the required receipt-level "Continue shopping" control findable: it sat under the order summary beside "View your orders," distinct from the header Shop link.
The receipt's "Continue shopping" control routed to Checkout instead of the catalog, leaving the shopper in an empty-cart payment flow with Cart 0 and a $6 total.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations, which may worsen visibility of quieter controls such as Remove or low-emphasis helper text.

findings.question: Did the order complete, and what did the receipt show?
findings.answer: Yes. The user reached order confirmation / receipt page `/order/o-1053`, showing order FF-1053 confirmed, Cart 0, an order summary, and receipt actions including "Continue shopping" and "View your orders." The completed purchase was Gentle Plant Food x3 rather than one unit because cart correction failed earlier.

findings.question: Where did the receipt's "Continue shopping" control take the user?
findings.answer: It took the user to Checkout at `http://127.0.0.1:4184/checkout`, not to the catalog/shop page.

findings.question: Was that destination appropriate after a finished order, or a loop / dead end?
findings.answer: It was inappropriate: after a finished order with Cart 0, Checkout showed an empty order summary with Subtotal $0.00, "Free shipping" $6.00, and Total $6.00, effectively returning the shopper to a payment flow with nothing to buy.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: Add to cart gave no immediate feedback while silently adding multiple units; cart quantity could not be edited despite copy promising it; Remove did not remove the line; checkout prefilled an invalid postcode; failed validation cleared payment fields; and shipping was labeled free while charging $6. These issues directly changed the order from one unit to three and made the final empty-cart checkout destination more confusing.

findings.note: The first three product cards were exactly where expected, immediately under the toolbar/category chips, and names/prices were clear enough to record without friction.
The Sort combobox was discoverable in the expected toolbar location next to the Sort label; the user changed it without hesitation.

Price sorting is functionally broken: selecting `Price: low to high` updates the combobox and URL to `?sort=price-asc`, but the grid stays in Featured order with Monstera $38, Snake Plant $26, and Golden Pothos $19 first while cheaper Terracotta Pot $14 remains later.
The optional `Price: high to low` check confirmed the same failure: URL/label changed to `?sort=price-desc`, but the grid still did not reorder, and Fiddle-Leaf Fig $52 did not move to the front.
The app gives no visual feedback that sorting has failed; the selected sort label changes, making the unchanged grid misleading rather than obviously stale or errored.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast violations across the run, which may reduce readability of the catalog controls or product details for some shoppers.

findings.question: What were the first three products/prices before sorting?
findings.answer: Monstera Deliciosa $38.00, Snake Plant $26.00, and Golden Pothos $19.00 in top-left grid order.

findings.question: What were the first three after sorting Price low to high?
findings.answer: They were unchanged: Monstera Deliciosa $38.00, Snake Plant $26.00, and Golden Pothos $19.00.

findings.question: Did the grid order actually change to match the selected sort?
findings.answer: No. Low-to-high did not put cheaper items first, and the optional high-to-low check also left the grid in the same Featured order.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Yes: the Sort control looked successful because the label and URL changed, but product order did not. A shopper selecting low-to-high would still see $38, $26, $19 before the $14 Terracotta Pot; selecting high-to-low still would not surface the $52 Fiddle-Leaf Fig first.

findings.note: Account was the user’s expected “home base” for order history, but it only exposed Profile and Shipping; no past orders, totals, line items, or shipment status appeared after full-page scrolling.
The global navigation never offered Orders, Order history, Track order, or a comparable status entry point, leaving the user to guess through Shop, product detail, and Cart.

The goal could not be completed: the UI let the user infer Gentle Plant Food at $12 from the catalog, but did not back the actual order contents, amount paid, order date, or shipping state with an order record.

The Gentle Plant Food product page was findable and matched the likely item, but it behaved only as a first-time shopping page with no “you bought this,” reorder, or order-status cue for a signed-in customer.
The empty cart used internal-sounding copy, “Cart collection returned 0 rows,” instead of a customer-facing empty state; this was noticeable during the last-resort search.
Footer support existed only as a small email address, with no Track order, support form, or order lookup link to recover from the missing order-history flow.
Accessibility scan found repeated color-contrast issues, which may further weaken discoverability of subtle links such as Account and footer support email.

findings.question: Could the user find the order at all, and how many wrong turns did it take?
findings.answer: No. They checked the expected Account page first, then took four plausible wrong turns: Shop, the Gentle Plant Food product page, Cart, and footer/support cues. Repeated Account scrolling added extra friction but did not reveal a hidden order section.

findings.question: What did the user conclude about the order's contents, cost, and status — and does the shop back each conclusion with something on screen?
findings.answer: They could only infer the likely item was Gentle Plant Food at $12 from the catalog/product page. The shop did not back that as an actual prior order, did not confirm what was paid, and gave no shipped/not-shipped status.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They hesitated and backtracked on Account because Profile and Shipping looked like the right signed-in area but no orders appeared above or below the fold. Confusion became explicit after Cart also showed no order path and only an empty-cart message.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Missing: order history/status on Account and any Orders/Track link in nav or footer. Misleading/frictional: the signed-in Account page implies the shop knows the customer but omits purchase history; Cart shows developer-ish empty-state copy. Accessibility also reported color-contrast violations that could make subtle recovery links harder to perceive.

findings.note: Category pills for Plants, Pots & Planters, and Care & Tools were found where expected and gave the user a clear way to assemble a plant + pot + care order.

Product-card and detail copy carried the comparison: “Great on a shelf,” drainage/saucer, reservoir, “back shelf,” care difficulty, watering cadence, and price all helped the user choose appropriate items.
Price sort repeatedly appeared selected and changed the URL, but cards did not reorder in Plants, Pots, or Care, weakening the price-comparison workflow the user explicitly cared about.
Using Shop from product pages reset category and sort state, forcing the user to reselect Plants/Pots/Care and re-find products after each comparison.
Add to cart did not provide visible confirmation or immediate badge updates, leading the user to click again and unintentionally create duplicate quantities for Pothos and Watering Can.
Cart says “Quantities update as you change them,” but Quantity is plain text with no stepper, input, or other way to change 2 to 1.
Remove did nothing on multiple cart lines, so the user could not correct unwanted duplicates and abandoned rather than checkout a $96 cart they did not choose.
Color contrast violations were present throughout the run; this matters especially because small signals like Cart count and Remove links were already easy to miss visually.

findings.question: Which tools for narrowing and comparing (categories, sorting, search) did the user find, and did each behave as they expected?
findings.answer: They found and used category pills for Plants, Pots & Planters, and Care & Tools successfully. Sorting was found and appeared selectable, but did not reorder cards despite URL/label changes. Search was visible but not needed. Shop navigation unexpectedly reset filters/sort after product-detail visits.

findings.question: Did the user compare options before choosing? What information did they lean on, and was any of it missing or unclear?
findings.answer: Yes. They compared Pothos vs Snake Plant, Terracotta vs Self-Watering, and Plant Food vs Watering Can. They leaned on price, shelf fit, pot size/drainage, care difficulty, watering guidance, and use-case copy. The main missing comparison aid was side-by-side support; the user kept the comparison mentally.

findings.question: As the cart grew, did its contents and totals always match what the user had chosen? Note any mismatch.
findings.answer: No. The user intended 1× Pothos, 1× Terracotta, 1× Watering Can, and Plant Food for about $67, but the cart reached 2× Pothos, 1× Terracotta, 2× Watering Can, no Plant Food, and subtotal $96. The mismatch came from duplicate adds plus no working correction path.

findings.question: Where, if anywhere, did the user hesitate, backtrack, or get confused — and what on the screen caused it?
findings.answer: They hesitated after Add clicks because the Cart badge stayed unchanged and no toast/loading/success state appeared. They backtracked repeatedly because Shop reset filters. They got stuck in Cart because quantity looked non-editable despite copy promising updates, and Remove links did not change the cart.

findings.question: Was anything broken, misleading, or missing that a real shopper would notice? Be specific.
findings.answer: Broken: Remove no-opped and sort did not reorder cards. Misleading: cart copy promised editable quantities, and Add-to-cart feedback implied nothing happened while items later appeared duplicated. Missing: quantity steppers/inputs, immediate add confirmation, persistent browse state, and a reliable way to recover from mistakes before checkout.
